squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_3_8: Foci of squamous cell carcinoma are located mainly on the face, scalp, and neck (about 70% of all cases). The remaining proportion falls on the skin of the trunk and limbs.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_4_1: With dermatoscopy of squamous cell carcinoma, the following signs are  visualized:
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_4_2: Telangiectasia in the peripheral part of the tumor
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_4_3: Inclusions in the form of small blood clots
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_4_5: The radial orientation of the vascular structures in the peripheral part of the tumor
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_4_6: Glomerular structures represented by foci of convoluted vessels
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_5_1: Differential diagnosis is carried out with such neoplasms as:
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_6_1: Squamous cell skin cancer is a malignant tumor with all the ensuing circumstances. Even after its removal, the risk of a return of the disease in the form of local relapse or the appearance of metastases remains. The later the treatment is carried out, that is, the larger the lesion focus (area, depth) by the tumor, the higher the risk of progression.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_6_2: Metastases most often appear in regional (closest to the tumor) lymph nodes, but their spread to other organs cannot be ruled out.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_6_3: Squamous cell carcinoma can appear both on healthy skin and on the background of existing benign or precancerous tumors. In the latter case, there is a certain degree of difficulty in timely differential diagnosis and detection of malignant transformation.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_6_4: In recent years, the incidence of SCC has been increasing: by about 10% in 5 years.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_7_1: If a suspicion is detected or the first signs of squamous cell skin cancer are detected, an oncologist should be consulted. The oncologist conducts additional specifying tests. In the absence of sufficient clinical data for an unambiguous diagnosis, sometimes the tactics of active dynamic observation is chosen. More often, a suspicious lesion or biopsy is performed, followed by histological examination.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_7_2: With histological confirmation of SCC, a standard list of examinations is assigned to search or exclude the presence of metastases, after which a special treatment plan is formed.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_7_3: In this regard, in patients with the presence of SCC, the risk of other malignant tumors increases – a regular thorough examination of the skin is recommended. When suspicious neoplasms are detected, a positive role is played by their photo fixation, which will subsequently determine even minor changes in appearance. In the same situations, an examination by a dermatologist or oncologist in the spring and autumn (before the beach season and after it) is indicated. Of great importance is the mapping of skin neoplasms, which greatly simplifies further observation, the search for new formations, or changes to existing ones.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_8_1: The main treatment method is surgical: wide excision of the tumor focus. This is the most effective method with a low risk of local recurrence.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_8_2: Another effective and universally recognized method is short-focus x-ray therapy (radiation therapy). It is usually used to treat foci up to 20 mm.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_8_3: The use of other methods of local exposure (laser removal or cryodestruction) even of the earliest forms is unacceptable. The tumor should be removed radically, within healthy skin, without damaging the tumor focus itself. Otherwise, the risk of both local relapse and metastasis increases.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_8_4: Today, methods are being developed for the local use of cytostatics (chemotherapy). However, there is no unequivocal opinion regarding such treatment due to the fact that these methods increase the duration of treatment of skin cancer, the cost, the damaging effect on the healthy surrounding skin and have dubious radicalism when used improperly. Such treatment should be carried out under the strict supervision of a specialist. On the other hand, local treatment with the help of certified and approved by oncologists means has a good cosmetic result.
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_9_1: Prevention of the appearance of squamous cell carcinoma of the skin and its progression is gentle and careful attitude to the skin:
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_9_1: Limitation of ultraviolet radiation (natural (sun) and artificial)
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_9_2: The use of protective creams during periods of active sun
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_9_4: Limitation or exclusion of ionizing radiation, occupational hazards
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_9_5: Compliance with safety measures when working with skin-damaging factors
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_li_9_6: Personal hygiene and basic awareness of skin tumors
squamous_cell.squamous_cell_desc_9_2: It also requires regular examination of the skin, timely consultation with a specialist in the event of external changes in skin tumors, and the removal of potentially dangerous neoplasms.

atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_1: Atopic dermatitis (syn: atopic eczema, endogenous eczema, diffuse neurodermatitis) is an acute, subacute or chronic inflammation of the epidermis and dermis, causing severe itching. A history or close relatives often have other allergic diseases (pollinosis, bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis). Refers to the so-called atopic disease. In Greek, “atopy” means “without place”; in medicine, this concept combines a hereditary predisposition to atopic dermatitis, bronchial asthma and allergic rhinitis.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1: In 60% of patients, the disease begins in the first year, most often in the third month of life.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_2: Men are somewhat more often affected in infancy and childhood, while in women it is more common in adolescence.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_3: 70% of patients have a history or close relatives with allergic rhinitis, pollinosis, bronchial asthma
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4: In most patients, the disease begins before the age of 12 years, in adulthood the debut of the disease occurs very rarely
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_5: The course is chronic, relapsing, with periodic exacerbations.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_6: Seasonal exacerbations of allergies to airborne allergens (such as pollen) are noted.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_2: Dry skin due to frequent washing of the body and hands.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_4: Hormonal shifts: pregnancy, menstruation, thyroid disorders.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_5: Infections: Staphylococcus aureus, group A streptococci, dermatophytosis, candidiasis, herpes.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_6: Parasitic diseases (ascariasis, giardiasis, opisthorchiasis, enterobiasis, toxocariasis)
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_7: Time of year: in temperate climates, there is an improvement in summer and an aggravation in winter.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_1_8: Clothing, especially woolen fabrics (itching increases after removal), woolen blankets, feather pillows.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_2_1: Allergic reactions of the immediate type: interaction of the allergen with IgE-
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_2_2: by antibodies fixed on the surface of basophils and mast cells leads to the activation of these cells and the release of vasoactive substances. The role of IgE in the pathogenesis of atopic dermatitis is not entirely clear, but it has been established that Langerhans cells (specialized process cells of the epidermis) carry high-affinity IgE receptors and appear to mediate an inflammatory skin response.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_3_1_2: The main symptom is skin itching. Constant scratching creates a vicious circle: itching -> scratching -> rash -> itching.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_3_2_2: the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck,
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_3_2_5: the back of the hands and feet,
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_3_2_6: In severe cases, a generalized lesion.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_1_1: Red spots with fuzzy borders, papules and plaques, often peeling.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_1_2: Widespread swelling (the skin looks puffy, puffy).
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_1_4: Excoriations are the result of scratching.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_1_5: Secondary infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_1_6: Pustules (usually pierced in the center by a hair).
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_1: Lichenization (thickening of the skin and increase of the skin pattern) is the result of constant scratching and rubbing.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_2: Many small papules on the site of hair follicles.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_3: Cracks are painful, especially on the palms, fingers and soles.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_4: Loss of the outer third of the eyebrows and hyperpigmentation of the eyelids are the result of scratching the eyes.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_5: Characteristic skin fold under the lower eyelid (Denny-Morgan lines) .
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_6: White dermographism is a very characteristic sign of atopic dermatitis: if you run a blunt object over the affected skin, after a few seconds because of capillary spasm, a white stripe appears.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_4_2_7: Common ichthyosis and follicular keratosis are detected in 10% of patients.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_heading_5_1: Peculiarities of atopic dermatitis in infants
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_5_1: In infants, atopic dermatitis is one of the most severe skin diseases.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_5_2: As a rule, there is a hereditary predisposition to allergic diseases. The most common allergens are food products.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_5_1_1: Skin is red and edematous, covered with vesicles; peeling, mottling, crusts, cracks.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_5_2_1: Individual areas of the body are affected. Typical localization is face (except lips) and extensor surfaces of extremities.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_heading_6_1: Peculiarities of atopic dermatitis in older children
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_6_1_1: Papules and plaques, lichenization, erosions, crusts.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_6_2_1: The most common are the ulnar fossa and the popliteal fossa.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_heading_7_1: Peculiarities of atopic dermatitis in adults
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_1: Atopic dermatitis in adults is a chronic disease with exacerbations,
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_2: which are often caused by emotional overload. Many patients suffered from atopic dermatitis in childhood, often accompanied by bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_1_1: Acute stage. Red plaques with fuzzy borders; often peeling. Excoriations appear due to scratching of skin. With secondary infection, pustules (usually pierced by hair in the center) and crusts appear.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_1_2: Chronic stage. Lichenization is a thickening of the skin with an intensification of the skin pattern, which appears due to constant scratching of the skin. Lichenization foci cover large areas of the skin or represent individual nodules (which can easily be confused with nodular scabies).
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_1_3: Aggravation. Papules and plaques, lichenization, exoriations, pustules, erosions, dry crusts or pustules, cracks.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_2_1: Generalized lesions are common. Typical localization: flexural surfaces of arms and legs, front and side surfaces of the neck, face (eyelids, forehead), wrists, rear surface of feet and hands.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_3_1: As the child grows older, there is usually a more or less stable remission. For adolescents, exacerbations, which are more severe, are characteristic. Most have the disease for 15-20 years. In 30-50% of them develop bronchial asthma or pollinosis. If atopic dermatitis begins in adulthood, it is very severe.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_7_4_1: Secondary staphylococcal infection results in extensive erosions and crusts. Kaposi’s herpetic eczema is a very severe, sometimes life-threatening complication caused by the herpes simplex virus.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_8_11: diseases of the immune system – Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, IgE hyperproduction syndrome, histiocytosis X (Letterer-Sivet syndrome), isolated IgA deficiency.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_desc_9_1: Anamnesis (onset in infancy) and clinical picture (typical localization and elements of rash, white dermographism).
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_10_1: Seeding: the nasal cavity and affected skin are often infected with Staphylococcus aureus. In the severe form of atopic dermatitis, carrier or secondary Staphylococcus aureus infection is detected in almost 90% of patients.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_10_2: Virus isolation in cell culture: if crusts are present, Kaposi’s herpetic eczema (the causative agent is herpes simplex virus) is ruled out.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_10_3: Determination of total IgE concentration in blood
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_10_4: Skin tests with allergens (prick test, scarification tests, intradermal tests).
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_10_6: Histological examination in doubtful cases: the epidermis contains acanthosis, expressed in varying degrees, occasionally spongiosis (intercellular edema). Dermal infiltrates contain lymphocytes, monocytes, mast cells; few or no eosinophils.
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_11_5: Treatment of combined allergic diseases (bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis)
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_11_6: Treatment of detected systemic and organ manifestations of atopic dermatitis (pathology of the gastrointestinal tract, urinary system, thyroid gland)
atopic_dermatitis.atopic_dermatitis_li_11_9: Educational programs for family members and patients

dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_1: Dermatitis (from the ancient Greek δέρμα, δέρματος – skin + Latin itis – to move, turn) – acute or chronic inflammation of the skin , developing at the site of direct exposure to an external physical or chemical factor.
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_2: This disease is very common, affecting 15-20% of all patients with skin diseases.
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_3: The diagnoses “dermatitis” and “eczema” are often used interchangeably. In the Anglo-American medical literature, the term “dermatitis” is more often used to refer to such diseases. In European dermatology, for many decades it has been customary to call intolerance skin reactions that occur acutely and have a tendency to rapid self-recovery – dermatitis , and chronically occurring with a weak tendency to self-recovery – eczema .
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_4: With this in mind, the following classification of dermatitis has been adopted :
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_2_1: The intensity of inflammation is related to the concentration of the irritant (irritant) and the duration of contact.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_4_1: with constant contact with weak stimuli
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_4_2: strong stimuli cause an immediate reaction
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_4_1: About 80% of cases of contact dermatitis are simple irritant contact dermatitis. Unlike allergic contact dermatitis, there is no allergic reaction to a specific allergen in the development of irritant contact dermatitis.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_1: Susceptibility to an irritant (irritant) is individual and may vary
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_2: Ways of exposure to the stimulus:
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_4: When the irritation threshold is reached, persistent dermatitis develops from minor contact with mild irritants.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_5: Low humidity lowers the irritation threshold.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_6: Exposure to moisture and the wet-dry cycle in areas such as the palms, buttocks, groin, and skin around a wound, and in infants, often causes inflammation.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_7: Irritant dermatitis can be complicated by allergies as the use of topical drugs increases, and also as a result of the easier penetration of allergens into damaged skin.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_5_8: Atopic background (hay fever, asthma or eczema) predisposes to increased susceptibility of the skin to irritation, dermatitis in such patients takes a long time and is more difficult to treat.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_6_1_1: dorsal and palmar surfaces of the hands
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_6_1_3: lips (often the habit of licking the lips leads to a repetitive wet-dry cycle)
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_6_1: Acute irritant dermatitis may present as weeping papules and/or vesicles on an erythematous patchy background with weeping and edema.
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_6_2: Persistent chronic irritant dermatitis is characterized by lichenification, erythematous macules, fissures, excoriations, and scaling. The hyperkeratotic form is characterized by persistent scaling, fissures, and mild erythema and may result from mechanical trauma, such as paper handling. Exposed skin may “burn” on contact with topical preparations that are otherwise well tolerated.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_7_1: Examination in KOH solution to exclude fungal infection
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_7_2: Patch test to assess the role of allergic contact dermatitis if its presence can be suggested from the history (eg, exposure to allergens) or if the disease is torpid and persists despite treatment and prevention measures. The patch test is usually performed using ready-made allergen screening lots consisting of 24 samples.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_7_3: Biopsy is rare and shows spongiosis, dermal edema, and an inflammatory, predominantly lymphocytic, infiltrate
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_8_1: Allergic contact dermatitis (vesicles and itching are often more typical of allergic contact dermatitis than simple irritant contact dermatitis).
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_1: Elimination or reduction of contact with skin irritants.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_2: Reducing the number of wet-dry cycles that occur due to, for example, constant handwashing.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_3: Cotton gloves worn under vinyl gloves help reduce hand wetness when working in wet environments.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_4: Appropriate gloves should be worn when handling specific solvents or chemicals.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_5: Regular application of softening emollients such as petroleum jelly to the affected skin.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_9_6: With simple irritant dermatitis of the hands, local hormonal agents are applied twice a day for several weeks – topical steroids of medium or high pharmacological efficacy to reduce erythema, itching, swelling and soreness.
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_10_1: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed-type allergic reaction that is caused by skin contact with an allergen. An allergy is specific to a particular chemical.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_10_1: metals such as nickel and chromium
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_10_2: rubber additives in the material of gloves and footwear ( carbamates , thiurams , mercapto-benzathiazole )
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_10_3: preservatives or other additives in skin lotions, sunscreens, other cosmetics and hygiene products
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_1: Contact with the chemical is necessary for the development of an allergy. After the initial contact, the development of hypersensitivity of the allergic type takes 14-21 days.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_2: The time required for the development of inflammation in a previously sensitized person is 12-48 hours, but can vary from 8-120 hours.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_3: After a single contact, the rash can last up to 3 weeks.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_4: Allergies to products (cosmetics, external medicines, allergens related to the patient’s profession) or to other substances can occur even if the patient has previously been in contact with them for a long time and without any difficulty.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_5: Eruptions recur if contacts are repeated.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_6: Because many products have the same or chemically similar ingredients, substituting one topical product for another often does not resolve the rash.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_7: Some patients develop contact allergies to several allergens at once (multiple).
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_8: Some allergen-causing substances are photoallergens: their interaction with sunlight is necessary for an allergic reaction to occur.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_9: Individuals sensitized to topical drugs or other allergens may develop generalized eczematous inflammation if drugs or other chemicals are ingested (intrinsic-external reaction). For example, a patient sensitized to topical diphenhydramine cream reacts with a generalized rash to oral diphenhydramine .
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_11_10: Strong sensitizers such as poison ivy can cause intense inflammation despite their low concentration or short contact; weak sensitizers can only cause pruritic erythema.
dermatitis.dermatitis_desc_12_1: The intensity of inflammation depends on individual degree of sensitivity, allergen concentration and from the duration of contact with the allergen.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_12_6: blisters (cause strong allergens like poison ivy)
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_1: The palms, forearms, and face are the most common sites for allergic contact dermatitis.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_2: Initially, dermatitis only affects the area of direct contact.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_3: If this contact is chronic, allergic dermatitis may spread beyond the area of primary contact.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_5: Allergy to a topical preparation applied to the face may present as asymmetrically itchy patches of erythema, and vesicles are rarely present.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_6: Allergic contact dermatitis can affect very limited areas of the skin, such as the eyelids, backs of the hands, lips, feet, or genitals.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_7: Airborne allergens (such as from burning poison ivy) can cause dermatitis on the face (including the eyelids and skin behind the ears), neck, and other exposed areas of the body.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_8: Photoallergic contact dermatitis typically affects exposed areas of the body: the face, neck, forearms, and backs of the hands. Areas under the chin, on the upper eyelids, and behind the ears are usually not affected.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_13_9: Occupational allergic contact dermatitis most commonly affects the palms; the face and eyelids may be affected if the allergen is airborne or there is indirect transmission of the allergen from the hands to the face.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_14_1: Flap testing is indicated for individuals with persistent or recurrent dermatitis. It is carried out with a fairly wide panel of allergens from the fields of professional activity and leisure, as well as those associated with skin care products. If the set of allergens for patch testing is limited or does not include allergens from the patient’s occupational area, some important allergens may be missed. Proper patch testing requires three visits to a dermatologist. The first is to apply the allergenic chemical at the appropriate concentration, the second is to take the test, read and analyze the results, and the last visit is for the final assessment of delayed reactions. If the last step is omitted, allergen identification may fail.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_14_2: Patchwork phototest is performed in patients with the distribution of the lesion according to the type of photodermatitis.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_15_2: Atopic dermatitis (the type of distribution of lesions can help in differentiation; atopic patients often have contact allergies).
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_15_4: Rosacea (erythema distribution, flushing, and presence of a burning sensation help to make a differential diagnosis).
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_1: For recovery, it is necessary to avoid contact with the allergen. It is important to correctly identify allergens. If the cause is not obvious, it is recommended to start treatment in order to conduct an examination later and schedule a patch test.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_2: All moisturizers, lotions and external agents are canceled, with the exception of plain petroleum jelly, if it is necessary for dry skin.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_3: Some allergens (such as those in hair color chemicals and adhesives) can penetrate rubber gloves, so this protection may not be adequate.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_4: For the treatment of dermatitis, corticosteroid ointment is prescribed twice a day for 2-3 weeks.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_5: The choice of pharmacological efficacy of a corticosteroid depends on which area of the body is affected: weak corticosteroids are used for the face, medium-strength corticosteroids for the arms, legs and trunk, and corticosteroids with high pharmacological efficacy for the palms and soles.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_6: It is preferable to use a corticosteroid ointment rather than a cream, since cream additives can be allergenic.
dermatitis.dermatitis_li_16_7: In the case of severe or generalized contact dermatitis, a course of systemic corticosteroids is prescribed for 3 weeks with a gradual decrease in dosage.

eczema.eczema_desc_1: Eczema is the common name for various inflammatory skin diseases characterized by severe itching, peeling and reddening of the skin, and dry or soaking rashes. Eczema is not transmitted by contact with a sick person. It can be acute or chronic, and in most cases is characterized by an improvement in the summer and a worsening in the winter.
eczema.eczema_desc_2: Acute eczema is characterized by itching, redness, swelling of the skin and the formation of transparent blisters. Chronic eczema is characterized by redness, a fine rash with peeling and cracking. Due to mechanical irritation from the itching, thickening of the skin is often formed, which cracks easily. Infection of the scratch with the development of microbial complications also occurs frequently.
eczema.eczema_desc_1_1: The emergence and development of the disease is provoked by a complex of different factors. There are primary and secondary factors.
eczema.eczema_li_1_9: chronic foci of infection in the body
eczema.eczema_li_1_10: use of unsuitable means for a particular person (household chemicals, perfumes, cosmetics, etc.)
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_1: The main symptom is the appearance of inflammatory foci with small blisters and pitting erosions, with mucous, scratching, crusting, and peeling.
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_3: In addition to foci of inflammation, there are scattered dry rashes on the body.
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_4: The boundaries of the foci are indistinct.
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_5: Rashes appear on the face and hands, spreading to the trunk and extremities. Symmetry of the lesions is pronounced.
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_6: The acute process turns into a chronic course, which is manifested by a cyclic development from exacerbations to relapses.
eczema.eczema_li_2_1_7: With a prolonged course, the skin in the lesion foci thickens and the skin pattern intensifies.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_1: Subjects with oily skin and increased sebum production.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_2: It is localized first on the scalp.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_3: It is observed in places with a large number of sebaceous glands – behind the ears, in the anatomical folds, on the folds, then passes to the neck and chest.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_4: The affected area has small yellow and pink nodules, crusts and scales, and swollen skin.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_5: In the scalp area, the hair is sticky with exudate, there are scales, crusts and redness. After removal of the crusts, there are soaking spots.
eczema.eczema_li_2_2_7: When skin folds are affected, cracks, swelling, and redness appear.
eczema.eczema_li_2_3_1: It occurs against the background of allergic reactions.
eczema.eczema_li_2_3_2: Exacerbations are characteristic of the spring and summer seasons or periods of great stress.
eczema.eczema_li_2_3_3: Adults under forty years of age are more susceptible, while children are less common.
eczema.eczema_li_2_3_4: The first symptoms affect the fingers – rashes begin to appear on the sides, and then they spread to the palms of the hands and feet.
eczema.eczema_li_2_3_6: As the disease progresses, exfoliation occurs.
eczema.eczema_li_2_4_1: It is characterized by the formation of severely itchy red, rounded plaques that become wet during periods of exacerbation.
eczema.eczema_li_2_4_2: It appears on various parts of the body, more often on the shins and forearms.
eczema.eczema_li_2_4_3: Accompanied by intense itching and peeling.
eczema.eczema_li_2_4_4: Is provoked by insect bites, scratches, dry skin, contact with nickel, disorders of blood supply to the lower extremities.
eczema.eczema_li_2_5_1: It is the result of increased sensitivity of the body to a microbial agent (streptococcus, staphylococcus, etc.) when pathogens get into open wounds on the skin.
eczema.eczema_li_2_5_2: Frequent provoking factors are disorders of the neuroendocrine and immune systems, gastrointestinal dysfunction.
eczema.eczema_li_2_5_3: The lesions have an asymmetric shape and distinct boundaries. Purulent crusts are formed with moist areas beneath them.
eczema.eczema_li_2_5_4: There is a strong itching sensation.
eczema.eczema_li_2_6_1: More often develops with varicose veins, obesity, heart and kidney failure, hypertension, endocrine disorders, including diabetes mellitus.
eczema.eczema_li_2_6_3: A feeling of heaviness and pain in my legs bothers me.
eczema.eczema_li_2_6_4: Redness and edema of the skin of the anterior surface of the shins form against a background of serous- purulent crusts with moist surfaces underneath.
eczema.eczema_li_2_7_1: It occurs with a predisposition to inflammatory diseases of the hair follicles.
eczema.eczema_li_2_7_2: It develops in places of increased hairiness – chin, upper lip, axillary area, pubis.
eczema.eczema_li_2_7_4: The formation of moist areas, pustules, and crusts is observed.
eczema.eczema_li_2_8_1: Provoked by regular contact with chemical irritants and microtraumas.
eczema.eczema_li_2_8_2: Zones of lesions are in places of contact with irritating agents, but it is also possible throughout the body.
eczema.eczema_li_2_8_3: The clinical picture is similar to true eczema.
eczema.eczema_li_2_8_4: Symptoms go away after contact with irritants is stopped.
eczema.eczema_li_2_9_1: Causes – hereditary predisposition in combination with other factors – parasitic infections, endocrine system diseases, irrational use of drugs (antibiotics and hormones), violation of the diet and the nature of nutrition, gastrointestinal diseases, contact with chemical irritants (household products, cosmetics).
eczema.eczema_li_2_9_3: There is redness and swelling of the skin, the formation of small blisters, as well as extensive blotchy lesions as the disease progresses.
eczema.eczema_li_2_9_4: With a prolonged course, the skin becomes drier and superficial cracks form.
eczema.eczema_li_3_3: Laboratory tests of blood, urine, and feces
eczema.eczema_li_3_5: Biochemical blood tests and other additional tests as indicated.
eczema.eczema_desc_3_1: The diagnosis is usually made clinically. Identification of atopic diseases in relatives helps to confirm the diagnosis.
eczema.eczema_desc_3_2: Differential diagnosis is made with allergic contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, scabies, vesicles, psoriasis, pyoderma, mycosis, atopic dermatitis.
eczema.eczema_desc_4_1: The patient is consulted and treated by a dermatologist. Strict adherence to his recommendations can significantly improve the condition and achieve persistent remission in the chronic course of the disease.
eczema.eczema_li_5_2: Establishment and elimination of provocative factors
eczema.eczema_li_5_4: Adherence to a hypoallergenic diet and lifestyle

onychomycosis.onychomycosis_desc_1: Onychomycosis refers to any nail infection caused by dermatophytes, non-dermatophytes or yeasts.
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_2_1: Distal (lateral) subungual onychomycosis – invasion through hyponychium, affects the distal part of the nail, spreads proximally until complete defeat
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_2_2: Proximal subungual onychomycosis – invasion under the proximal nail fold with damage to the proximal part of the nail plate
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_2_3: White superficial onychomycosis – direct invasion of the nail plate: causes the appearance of white or dull yellow sharply bordered spots on the surface of the nail
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_desc_3: Clinical types of nail lesions, depending on the degree of thickening of the nail plate:
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_3_1: Normotrophic: there is only a yellow or white discoloration of the nail plate
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_3_2: Hypertrophic: thickening and formation of ridges on the nail plate, hypertrophy of the underlying tissues (nail bed)
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_3_3: Atrophic: thinning and detachment of the nail plate.
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_desc_4: Atrophic: thinning and detachment of the nail plate.
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_li_4_3: Laboratory diagnostics: microscopy, culture method, PCR
onychomycosis.onychomycosis_desc_5: Various complex systemic and local antifungal agents are used to treat onychomycosis. Systemic treatment is required in all cases where there is a lesion of the scalp, beard and nails. With limited skin lesions without affecting the appendages of the skin, external monotherapy can be used.

pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_1: Pityriasis versicolor is a chronic mycosis caused by fungi of the genus Malassezia, most commonly M. furfur. It can exist as a saprophyte, a yeast-like type that is a normal inhabitant of sebum-rich skin areas, and as a pathogen, an “activated” mold-like (mycelial) type that causes shingles.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_2: Factors responsible for mycelial transformation include a warm, humid environment, use of oral contraceptives, heredity, use of systemic corticosteroids, Cushing’s disease, immunosuppression, hyperhidrosis and malnutrition.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_1_1: The most common manifestations of Pityriasis versicolor are flaky, pigmented (noninflammatory) patches of pink, yellow, brown, and coffee and milk. In dark-skinned individuals, they are lighter in color than the surrounding skin.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_2_1: The face, scalp, and genitals are less frequently affected, and in severe cases, the process may spread to extensive areas.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_2_2: Borders are clearly delineated. The spots are up to 1 cm in size, but they tend to coalesce, forming large lesion foci. Presented complaints, as a rule, have an aesthetic character. Itching is moderate or absent. A secondary hypopigmentation (reversible) remains after tanning.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_2_3: The disease may also manifest as itchy folliculitis in the back, chest, and sometimes on the extremities. The primary rashes are perfollicular, erythematous, in the form of papules or pustules 2-3 mm in diameter. Only appropriate culture and KOH (potassium hydroxide) testing can distinguish this infection from bacterial folliculitis.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_li_3_1: Wood lamp – yellow or orange glow
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_li_3_2: KOH microscopy – detection of filamentous mycelium and globular pseudomycelium (a “meatball-spaghetti” appearance)
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_4_1: Antiseptics and antifungal agents in the form of shampoos, solutions or creams (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, terbinafine) are used to treat mild forms 2 times a day for 2-4 weeks.
pityriasis_versicolor.pityriasis_versicolor_desc_4_2: Therapy for severe forms includes systemic itraconazole (100 mg twice daily) or fluconazole (50 mg once daily) or ketoconazole (200 mg twice daily) for 2-4 weeks.

skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_1: Skin mycoses are a large group of fungal diseases caused by dermatophytes – filamentous fungi from the genera Epidermophyton, Trichophyton, Microsporum, etc. These fungi are widespread in nature, have a pronounced contagiousness and can be divided into:
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_1: Geophilic – transmitted by direct contact with soil, affect people sporadically, usually spread by spores that can live for years
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_2: Zoophilic – transmitted from animals through direct contact, or indirect – through objects on which there is contaminated animal hair
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_3: Anthropophilic – transmitted from person to person through direct contact or through household items
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_4: There are the following types of mycosis of the skin: tinea corporis (mycosis of the trunk), tinea manus (mycosis of the hands), tinea pedis (mycosis of the feet), tinea cruris (mycosis of the groin area).
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_1_1: Smooth skin mycoses include all skin mycoses of the trunk and extremities, with the exception of hair, nails, palms, soles and folds. It can appear on any part of the body. More common in tropical regions. Any dermatophyte can potentially cause smooth skin dermatophytosis, but the most common pathogens are Microsporum canis (zoophilic) and Tr. rubrum (anthropophilic).
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_1_2: The clinical picture is presented by many variants of mycosis of smooth skin. The classic manifestations are ring-shaped eruptions with scales along the entire erythematous border. The border is usually vesicular and thickens towards the center. The center of the rash is usually scaly. The rash can be “creeping” and ring-shaped.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_1: Fungal lesions of the palmar and plantar surfaces and interdigital spaces. It is the most common dermatomycosis worldwide.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_2: The most common pathogens are Tr. rubrum, rare cases: Tr. mentagrophytes, E. flocossum.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_4: Latent type – represented by mucous peeling in the folds of the palms and soles without inflammation, itching and thickening of the skin.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_5: Chronic hyperkeratotic type (“mocassin” type) – affects the soles, lateral and medial sides of the feet: the skin is dry, covered with pityriasis scales with areas of hyperkeratosis, cracks, itching can be expressed.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_6: Interdigital type (chronic intertriginous type, “athletic foot”) – affects the interdigital spaces of the feet, especially between the three lateral toes. Manifested by itchy erythema, peeling, painful cracks between the toes. An unpleasant odor may appear, spread to the soles or the back of the foot.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_7: Vesiculo-bullous type (dyshidrotic) – manifested by tense vesicles with a diameter of 2-3 mm, rarely – vesiculopustules and blisters on the skin of the soles and peri-plantar space.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_2_8: Acute ulcerative type is a complication of the interdigital or vesicular-bullous type with a secondary infection, most often caused by gram-negative microorganisms. Causes the formation of vesiculopustules and extensive festering ulceration on the plantar surface. The condition is often accompanied by cellulitis, lymphangitis, lymphadenopathy, and fever.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_3_1: Dermatophytic infection affecting the groin folds.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_3_2: Typical location: intergluteal, groin folds, inner thighs, pubic region.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_3_3: Pathogens: the most common and specific – Epidermophyton flocossum, less often – Trichophyton rubrum.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_3_5: Mycosis of folds usually manifests itself as multiple erythematous papullovesicles with well-defined convex borders. Itching is common, as is pain with maceration and secondary infection.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_4_1: Candidiasis is a group of diseases caused by yeast-like fungi of the genus Candida. Unlike molds, Candida forms a pseudomycelium.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_4_2: The most common causative agent of candidiasis – Candida albicans – a conditionally pathogenic microorganism, saprophyte, is present as a commensal organism in the vaginal mucosa in 20-25% of healthy women who do not present complaints, also colonizes in the oropharynx in 50% of healthy individuals, it is also possible to isolate Candida albicans in intertriginous areas of healthy people.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_4_3: Epidemiology: infection is possible through direct contact, sexually, through household items. The most likely reason is the activation of endogenous infection due to predisposing factors:
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_4_1: Immunodeficiencies (HIV, hyperimmunoglobulinemia E, chronic granulomatous disease, etc.)
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_4_2: Nutritional factors (vitamin deficiency, general malnutrition, iron deficiency)
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_4_4: Taking certain medications (immunosuppressants, cytostatics, steroids, antibiotics, etc.)
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_4_5: Hot and humid environment, skin trauma, dentures, tight clothing, etc
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_5_1: C. albicans tends to colonize skin folds: inguinal, axillary, submammary, intergluteal, interdigital, diaper area.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_5_2: It looks like itchy, erythematous, macerated “flaming” spots (sometimes – erosive papules) with satellite vesiculopustular, easily turning into erosion. A special type is prickly heat, which affects the back of bedridden patients and looks like isolated vesiculopustular containing yeast.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_1: Disseminated candidiasis – candidal sepsis (hematogenous spread). Fungi of the genus Candida can get hematogenous access from the oropharynx or gastrointestinal tract, if the function of the mucous barrier is impaired.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_2: With disseminated candidiasis, internal organs are affected. An increase in body temperature and a violation of the general condition are often observed.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_3: Some patients may also have skin lesions: erythematous papules 0.5–1.0 cm in size with a hemorrhagic or pustular center, and necrotic foci may appear. The lesions are located on the trunk and limbs, the number of rashes varies.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_4_2: Microscopy of samples (scraping) from the skin, treated with 10% KOH and stained before examination: identification of oval budding cells, elongated filamentous cells, connected end-to-end (pseudohyphae)
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_4_3: Cultivation on Sabouraud agar supplemented with antibiotics: whitish mucoid colonies grow within 2–5 days
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_6: For each type of candidiasis, there are affordable and effective treatments.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_7: With local damage (if the immune status is not compromised), apply:
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_7_1: Creams, ointments, solutions with drugs such as nystatin, levorin or natamycin, applied 1-2 times a day for 1-2 weeks
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_6_8: With a widespread process, ineffectiveness of local treatment, chronic course or immunodeficiency:
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_8_1: Itraconazole 100 mg – 2 times a day for 1-2 weeks; or 200 mg – 2 times a day for 1 week
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_8_2: Fluconazole 150 mg – once a week (once or for 2-4 weeks); or 50 mg – 1 time per day for 1-2 weeks
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_6_8_3: Ketoconazole 200 mg – 1 time per day for 1-2 weeks
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_1: Tinea versicolor is a chronic mycosis caused by fungi of the genus Malassezia, most commonly M. furfur. It can exist as a saprophyte – a yeast-like type that is a normal inhabitant of areas of the skin rich in sebum, and as a pathogen – an “activated” mold-like (mycelial) type that causes tinea versicolor.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_2: Factors responsible for mycelium transformation include warm, humid environments, oral contraceptive use, heredity, systemic corticosteroid use, Cushing’s disease, immunosuppression, hyperhidrosis, and undernutrition.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_4: The most common manifestations of tinea versicolor are flaky, pigmented (non-inflammatory) patches of pink, yellow, brown, coffee with milk. For dark-skinned people, it is lighter than the surrounding skin.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_5: Location: chest, back, abdomen and proximal extremities. Less commonly, the face, scalp and genitals are affected; in severe cases, the process can spread to large areas.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_6: Borders are clearly demarcated. The size of the spots is up to 1 cm, but they tend to merge, forming large lesions. The complaints presented are usually of an aesthetic nature. Moderate or no itching. After sunburn, secondary hypopigmentation (reversible) remains.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_7_7: It can also present with itchy folliculitis in the back, chest, and sometimes extremities. Primary eruptions are perfollicular, erythematous, in the form of papules or pustules 2-3 mm in diameter. Only appropriate culture and KOH test can distinguish this infection from bacterial folliculitis.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_7_8_1: Wood’s lamp – yellow or orange glow
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_li_7_8_2: KOH microscopy – identification of filamentous mycelium and spherical pseudomycelium (type of “meatballs-spaghetti”)
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_8_1: For the treatment of milder forms, antiseptics and antifungal agents are used in the form of shampoos, solutions or creams (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, terbinafine) 2 times a day for 2-4 weeks.
skin_mycoses.skin_mycoses_desc_8_2: Severe therapy includes systemic itraconazole (100 mg twice a day) or fluconazole (50 mg once a day) or ketoconazole (200 mg twice a day) for 2-4 weeks.

trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_1: Trichomycosis is a collective term that includes a group of diseases occurring with damage to hair follicles and hair. There are the following types of trichomycosis: tineacapitis (mycosis of the scalp) and tineabarbae (mycosis of the beard area). The main cause of trichomycosis is the appearance on the skin of dermatomycete fungi of the genus Microsporum and Trichophyton.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_1_1: Tineacapitis – dermatophytosis of the scalp and hair in this area. Refers to infectious “quarantine” mycoses, epidemic outbreaks are possible. It is caused by any pathogenic dermatophytes from the genus Trichophyton and Microsporum, with the exception of T. concentricum. M. canis is the most common pathogen in the world, followed by T. tonsurans.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_1_2: Various clinical manifestations depend on the type of pathogen and the degree of the body’s immune response. There are two possible patterns of microorganism invasion:
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_1_1: Ectotrix – small and large fungus spores (arthroconidia) spread outside the hair shaft
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_1_2: Endotrix – arthroconidia remain inside the hair shaft
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_1: Non-inflammatory (superficial) type – usually caused by anthropophilic fungi: endotrix Tr. tonsurans (“trichophytosis”) or ectotrix M. Ferrugineum, M. Canis (“microsporia”).
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_2: Skin: minimal inflammation (round, pink-red or dull red, well-defined patches) or absent (non-inflammatory or seborrheic type with visible flaking and hyperkeratosis). Lesions are relatively small, multiple, located in the marginal region of the scalp, but may coalesce into large areas that involve the entire scalp.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_3: Hair can be visually intact. At the same time, the affected area often looks like a well-defined round area of ​​alopecia (hair is broken off at the very base), hyperkeratosis and peeling are noted. The appearance resembles a “wheat field”. Preserved hair and scales emit a greenish glow in Wood’s lamp.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_4: The inflammatory type is usually noted when infected with zoophilic Tr fungi. Gypseum and M. Canis. It manifests itself in the form of 1-3 relatively large foci of inflammation. The spectrum of inflammation ranges from pustular folliculitis to kerion, which is a deep inflammation center dotted with broken hair and follicular orifices from which pus flows. Hair can be easily removed. The consequence of this inflammation can lead to cicatricial alopecia.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_5: Black dot dermatophytosis is caused by anthropophilic Trichophytons. This is the least inflammatory form of ringworm on the head. The affected areas are usually multiple, with uneven edges, covered with small scales. In some cases, hair loss may not occur. However, when this happens, the hair in the lesion breaks off inside the mouth, leaving black spots on the scalp. The process can lead to atrophic alopecia.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_2_6: Tineabarbae – damage to the skin and hair in the area of beard or mustache growth in men. Most often caused by zoophilic microorganisms T. mentagrophytes and T. verrucosum and, in rare cases, M. canis.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_3_1: The inflammatory type (purulent, parasitic sycosis) – usually caused by T. mentagrophytes and T. Verrucosum, completely repeats the inflammatory type of tineacapitis before the formation of kerion.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_3_2: The superficial type is a form of mycosis of the beard caused by anthropophils, with a less pronounced inflammatory process, reminiscent of bacterial folliculitis with mild diffuse erythema.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_3_3: Annular type – repeats tineacorporis, manifests itself as annular lesions with slightly raised inflammatory edges, covered with vesiculopustules and crusts, with central desquamation.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_4_1: The diagnosis of trichomycosis is based on clinical evidence and epidemiological investigation. Various instrumental studies are used to confirm the diagnosis:
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_4_1: Luminescent method (carried out using a special Wood lamp, emitting a special spectrum of ultraviolet illumination, in which a fungal infection of the skin and hair acquires a characteristic glow depending on the type of pathogen)
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_4_2: Microscopic examination of pathological material (examination of hair or skin scales under a microscope to detect specific signs of fungal infection)
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_4_4: PCR diagnostics (study of fungal DNA in biological material).
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_4_2: In addition to clinical significance, accurate diagnosis and identification of the type of pathogen is necessary to determine the scope of anti-epidemic measures.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_5_1: Differential diagnosis of trichomycosis is carried out:
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_5_1: Between different types of trichomycosis, depending on the pathogen
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_1: When the first signs of trichomycosis appear, it is necessary to consult a dermatologist. Only in conjunction with a specialist can you choose the right treatment, which will not only avoid the progression of the disease in a given patient with the development of unpleasant complications, but also exclude the transmission of the pathogen to people around them.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_2: For the treatment of trichomycosis, both local and systemic treatment is used. The main treatment is systemic (tablets, capsules, suspensions). Local treatment is optional. Local treatment can be independent with small lesions and the absence of pronounced clinical manifestations.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_3: The most common antifungal drug for the treatment of trichomycosis is griseofulvin (for systemic use). The drug is quite safe, therefore it is also used in children (there is a dosage form in the form of a suspension). In addition to griseofulvin, terbinafine or itraconazole are prescribed.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_4: With frequent episodes of trichomycosis (which indicates a weakened immune system), vitamin therapy, immunotherapy, and other drugs are prescribed to eliminate trigger factors.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_5: With severe itching, antihistamines can be used, with the addition of a microbial infection – antibacterial drugs.
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_6: The following are used as local treatments:
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_6_1: Antifungal ointments (Mikospor, Miconazole, Exoderil, Lamisil and others, including those prepared in a pharmacy)
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_6_2: 2–5% iodine tincture for treatment of lesions
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_li_9_3: Lotions containing salicylic acid, quinosol and dimexide in the composition (prepared in the pharmacy)
trichomycosis.trichomycosis_desc_6_7: In addition to medications, for the entire period of treatment, it is necessary to adhere to weekly shaving of the scalp and washing the head with hot water and soap 2-3 times a week. It is also recommended to cover your head with a gauze bandage during the day (the bandages are burned in the evening) and to minimize close contact with people, especially children, to exclude the sharing of hygiene products and clothing.

devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1: Devergie’s lichen is a rare chronic inflammatory skin disease with unknown etiology. The main manifestations of this pathology include peeling and redness of the skin in combination with damage to the hair follicles. Equally common in both men and women, and without emphasis on age.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_2: There are 6 clinical types of Devergie’s lichen:
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_1: Type I is the most common, which is also called the “classic adult type”. This type of Devergie’s lichen has the best prognosis, since up to 80% of cases pass on their own within 3 years
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_2: Type II – atypical, is a type I variety, which is characterized by atypical onset of the disease in adults
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_3: Types III, IV, and V are classic, limited, and atypical adolescent Devergie’s lichen
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_4: Type VI is an HIV-associated type of Devergie’s lichen
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3: Considering the non-infectious nature of Devergie’s lichen, it is not contagious and is not transmitted from person to person. Devergie’s lichen is usually not inherited, but familial cases associated with a genetic predisposition have been described.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_1: The main manifestation of Devergie’s lichen is a characteristic pinpoint rash, which in the early stages can be accompanied by the appearance of itching. As the disease worsens, thick skin appears on the palms and soles, followed by peeling, cracks and soreness. This can make walking difficult, and working with your hands causes noticeable discomfort.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_2: Further progression of the rash can cause a fever, severe weakness, and other signs of intoxication. Elements of the rash merge into large red spots.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_3: Signs of the most common Devergie’s lichen (type I):
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_1_1: The rash usually begins suddenly on the scalp and spreads to most of the chest and abdomen;
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_1_2: The spots are dry, scaly, red with an orange tinge and well-defined edges. Smaller patches may coalesce to cover larger areas of the skin
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_li_1_3: Between the larger red spots, areas of normal skin can often be seen
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_4: The hair follicles on the affected skin areas are enlarged, denser to the touch, with a scaly surface due to hyperkeratosis.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_5: The skin on the palms and soles may thicken and be orange in color. Nails may also thicken with subsequent discoloration and, in severe cases, hair loss.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_6: Type II (atypical adult) accounts for 5% of all cases of Devergie’s lichen and does not have the classic course described above, when the rash begins in the head. Here, the legs are usually immediately affected with thickening of the skin on the palms and soles. Devergie’s lichen type II may be associated with increased hair loss.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_7: Type III accounts for 10% of all cases. The manifestations are similar to those of type I, but they begin in childhood.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_8: Type IV accounts for 25% of cases. Symptoms are similar to those of type II, but are also typical for children.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_9: Type V accounts for 5% of cases. Combines the symptoms of type I and type II, but the disease is noted in several members of the same family. This type has an autosomal dominant inheritance with the manifestation of the first symptoms in childhood. It usually starts with dry skin and blockage of hair follicles, later thickening of the skin on the arms and legs joins.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_1_10: Type VI occurs in people with HIV and is characterized by red, scaly patches around hair follicles with or without involvement of the palms and soles.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_2_1: A visual examination is often sufficient to diagnose Devergie’s lichen. However, the diagnosis process can be difficult if the rash is atypical. If the diagnosis is unclear, additional tests may be done to rule out fungal skin lesions (potassium hydroxide (KOH test) or other diseases (culturing, biopsy).
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_2_2: The various types of hairy scalp can look like psoriasis and are often mistaken for psoriasis, especially in the early stages.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_1: There are no standardized treatment protocols for Devergie’s lichen treatment, as well as specific medications. Topical and systemic therapies are usually used alone or in combination.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_2: For small areas of skin lesions, local treatment is prescribed. Steroid creams and ointments can reduce the severity of symptoms (redness, flaking, itching) but do not change the duration of the illness.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_3: Moisturizing topical medicines are a very important part of the treatment, helping to relieve dryness and restore the skin’s barrier function. Emollients should be used regularly.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_4: In the case of extensive lesions and the occurrence of general symptoms of intoxication, a dermatologist, after assessing the patient’s condition, prescribes systemic treatment. The most commonly used are retinoids, methotrexate, and systemic corticosteroids.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_5: To relieve itching, antihistamines, both local and systemic, can be prescribed. In some cases, phototherapy (light therapy) is used.
devergie_lichen.devergie_lichen_desc_3_6: If the drugs listed above are ineffective, as well as the progression of the rash, biological drugs can be used that act on specific antibodies that block a certain protein involved in the occurrence of Devergie’s lichen. These drugs include infliximab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, and adalimumab.

lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_1: Lichen nitidus is a fairly rare chronic skin disease of unknown origin and development mechanism, in which shiny granulomas appear on the surface of the skin – dense nodules of small sizes. Lichen nitidus rarely causes other symptoms and usually does not require treatment. Lichen nitidus is not contagious and rarely comes with any complications.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_2: Lichen nitidus occurs in the age group over 10 years old equally often in both men and women. However, at the age of 3-10 years, it is mainly typical for boys.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_1_1: The reasons for the appearance of Lichen nitidus are unclear. Some experts believe that Lichen nitidus is an autoimmune disease, but the evidence base in this regard is insufficient.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_1_2: Skin conditions such as vitiligo or psoriasis can also increase the likelihood of developing shingles.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_1_3: Lichen nitidus is often considered as an infectious-allergic skin disease. This is due to the fact that Lichen nitidus is often detected in the presence of focal infection, as well as the positive effect of antibiotic therapy. The tendency to atopic dermatitis in patients with Lichen nitidus indicates a high likelihood of an allergic component in the etiology of Lichen nitidus.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_1_4: The following are considered as possible triggers for the appearance of Lichen nitidus:
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_li_1_4: The presence of severe concomitant pathology, especially those conditions that lead to suppression of the human immune system
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_2_1: Lichen nitidus is characterized by the appearance of small round nodules on the skin with a diameter of 1-3 millimeters. These nodules do not coalesce into one large patch, but may clump together to form more intense areas of the rash (areas of congestion). The top of the rash element (nodule) is flattened, the nodule itself is flesh-colored, but its surface is smooth, which gives the impression of shine.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_2_2: Clusters of the rash usually appear on:
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_li_2_3: In the area of ​​the upper and lower extremities
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_li_2_5: In rare cases – on the palms and soles
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_2_3: Lichen nitidus usually has no other symptoms. However, in some people, the rash may be itchy.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_3_1: To diagnose Lichen nitidus, visual examination and anamnesis of the disease are often sufficient. However, the diagnosis process can be difficult if the rash is atypical. If the diagnosis is unclear, additional tests may be done to exclude fungal skin lesions (potassium hydroxide (KOH test) or other conditions (dermatoscopy, culturing, biopsy).
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_4_1: A rash with  Lichen nitidus can be similar to the rash seen in other skin conditions: atypical manifestations of psoriasis, molluscum contagiosum, milia, comedones.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_4_2: A similar rash may be a manifestation of intolerance to certain medications or exposure to other toxic substances on the body.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_4_3: A rash on your knees, elbows, soles, or palms can be a sign of more serious medical conditions than  Lichen nitidus.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_5_1: Lichen nitidus usually does not require treatment. The rash usually goes away within a few months. Treatment may be recommended when symptoms appear that significantly impair quality of life. However, such situations are quite rare.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_5_2: In this case, the following are assigned:
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_5_3: Consultation of a specialist (dermatologist) is mandatory when the first signs of Lichen nitidus appear, with a progressive course of the disease, with the occurrence of other symptoms (redness of the skin, itching). This is necessary in order to promptly exclude other, more severe, but similar in the course of the disease, as well as to begin treatment if necessary.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_6_1: Lichen nitidus rarely causes any complications. The only unpleasant moment can be a feeling of embarrassment and awkwardness in severe cases, when large areas of the skin are affected.
lichen_nitidus.lichen_nitidus_desc_6_2: Sometimes visible changes in the skin, especially in children and adolescents, can cause various mental disorders, such as depression or anxiety disorder due to a cosmetic defect.

lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_1: Lichen planus (LP) is an inflammatory skin disorder characterized by an itchy, non-infectious rash on the hands and feet. The rash consists of small, multifaceted, flat, pink or purple papules with a flat surface.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_1_1: The definite cause of lichen planus is unknown. The following are considered as possible triggers for the appearance of the LP:
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_1_1: Certain medicines, including some medicines for the treatment of hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, and malaria
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_1: Lichen planus symptoms vary depending on which part of the body is affected.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_2: With skin lesions, the most common symptom is the presence of shiny red or purple papules 3-5 mm in symmetrical areas of the body. The number of elements of the rash can vary from single to multiple. Papules, as a rule, are somewhat harder than the surrounding skin, and itching of varying degrees of intensity may be present in their area. On the surface of the papule, peeling or whitish striation (Wickham striae) can be found. Edges are uneven, polycyclic.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_3: The rash occurs anywhere but is most common on the wrists, arms, back, and ankles. More pronounced, thickened scaly patches may appear on the shins and ankles. One of the characteristic signs of LP is the appearance of new elements of the rash on the injured skin areas (scratches, abrasions, bites, etc.). Elements of the rash can coalesce to form large lesions.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_4: When the oral cavity is affected, lichen planus looks like lacy spots of small white dots. These spots can appear on the inside of the cheeks or on the tongue. In severe cases, itching, soreness, redness of the surrounding mucous membrane, ulceration join.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_5: Lichen planus can also appear on the nails of the hands and feet. Both individual nail plates and all nails are affected at the same time. Thinning, splitting, deformation up to destruction of the nail plate is observed.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_6: On the scalp, lichen planus is manifested by reddening of the skin, the appearance of red pinpoint papules, and itching. In some cases, the hair may start to thin out. In advanced cases, there is focal alopecia (lack of hair).
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_2_7: In the genital area, lichen planus causes bright red painful spots or papules.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_3_1: A rash with lichen planus may be similar to the rash seen with other skin conditions, including ringworm, tinea versicolor, pityriasis rosea, eczema, and psoriasis.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_3_2: A similar rash can be a manifestation of intolerance to certain medications or exposure to other toxic substances on the body.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_3_3: A rash on the palms or soles of the feet can be a sign of a more serious condition than pityriasis rosea. In such situations, a dermatologist’s examination is required.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_4_1: A visual examination is often sufficient to diagnose lichen planus. However, the diagnosis process can be difficult if the rash is atypical. If the diagnosis is unclear, additional tests may be done to exclude fungal skin lesions (potassium hydroxide (KOH test) or other diseases (culturing, biopsy).
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_5_1: Lichen planus is not a dangerous disease and usually goes away on its own.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_5_2: If there is severe itching, ulceration (more often it concerns the LP of the oral cavity or genital area), then in this case, symptomatic treatment is prescribed. Special measures are also indicated in the case of localization of LP in the area of ​​the scalp, in order to avoid irreversible hair loss. In these situations, on the recommendation of a dermatologist, the following are prescribed:
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_5_2: Local steroid drugs to reduce the intensity of the inflammatory process
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_5_5: Tacrolimus or other medicines used for eczema.
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_5_3: There is no specific treatment for lichen planus, as well as the prevention of its occurrence. However, there are a number of measures that allow you to avoid the progression of the rash, reduce its clinical manifestations and improve the quality of life:
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_5_6: Elimination or minimization of possible skin injuries
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_5_7: Timely treatment of already existing skin lesions
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_li_5_9: With lichen planus of the oral cavity, reduce to a minimum or, if possible, complete smoking cessation, exclusion of alcohol consumption, mild nutrition (exclusion of thermal and mechanical irritants), full oral hygiene
lichen_planus.lichen_planus_desc_5_4: In the absence of symptoms that worsen the quality of life and cause special discomfort, treatment is not required.

lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_1: Linear lichen – also known as acquired linear inflammatory skin rash, Blashko’s versicolor or linear lichenoid dermatosis with a fairly characteristic clinical picture. This is a benign, inflammatory skin disease that usually does not require treatment as it goes away on its own.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2: Linear lichen is a rare disease that most often occurs in children aged 5 to 15 years, although it can occur at any other age. The average age of onset of pathology is about 3 years.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_1_1: The exact cause of linear lichen is unknown. Some studies show a higher incidence among girls, but this has not been unequivocally proven, as well as the hereditary nature of this pathology.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_1_2: The most likely triggers for the development of linear lichen are:
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_li_1_4: Taking medications in pregnant women (especially antibacterial drugs)
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_li_1_6: Propensity to allergies (aggravated history of allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma or atopic dermatitis and other hypersensitivity reactions)
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_li_1_7: Environmental factors (seasonality is noted with exacerbations in the spring-summer period)
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_li_1_8: In the etiology of linear lichen, autoimmune processes are not excluded, especially those occurring during the intrauterine life of the subject. This connection is found for the reason that linear lichen corresponds to the Blaschko lines, which are of embryonic origin
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_1: Linear lichen is pinkish-red or flesh-colored spots formed by papules with a flat top and scaling, which gradually (within 2-3 weeks after appearance) merge with each other to form a characteristic scaly strip from a few centimeters to 20-30 cm long.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_2: In patients prone to atopic dermatitis, itching of varying intensity appears in the area of ​​the strip. It usually does not affect the quality of life. In severe cases, especially with severe cases of any other allergic reactions, itching is severe and requires medical correction.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_3: Lichene lesion usually occurs on the upper (more common) or lower extremities, although it can occur or extend to the neck, trunk, or buttocks. Rarely, primary lesions are located on the face or abdominal wall.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_4: Although lichen lineus predominantly affects the skin, it can also occur on the nails (in isolation or in combination with skin lesions). At the same time, onycholysis, splitting, abrasion and complete loss of the nail are noted.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_5: After the onset, the symptoms of linear lichen can persist for several months, after which they slowly disappear on their own. The entire period of the disease usually does not exceed one year. Relapses are rare.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_2_6: In place of the lichen, a strip of hyperpigmentation may remain, which disappears without a trace in 3-4 years. In rare cases, this streak persists for life.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_3_1: For the diagnosis of linear lichen, visual examination and anamnesis of the disease are often sufficient. However, the diagnosis process can be difficult if the rash is atypical. If the diagnosis is unclear, additional tests may be done to rule out fungal skin lesions (potassium hydroxide (KOH test) or other conditions (dermatoscopy, biopsy).
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_4_1: Linear lichen treatment is usually not required, as it goes away on its own within 3-12 months. Occasionally, topical medications may be prescribed to relieve local symptoms.
lichen_lichen.lichen_lichen_desc_4_2: Moisturizing oils or creams can be used to combat dry and itchy skin. Local steroids are also used.

pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_1: Pityriasis rosea is a type of skin rash. The disease begins with one large, round or oval pink spot measuring about 2 cm or more (the so-called maternal plaque). Over time, the maternal plaque begins to turn yellow, as if wrinkling, peeling appears.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2: After a few days, other, smaller (usually no more than 1 cm) pink spots begin to appear on the body. The rash most commonly appears on the chest, back, and abdomen in people between the ages of 10 and 35. The period from the appearance of the maternal plaque to the disappearance of the last spot is approximately 1-3 months.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_3: In the normal course, Pityriasis rosea, as a rule, does not cause serious complications and is not transmitted from person to person by contact.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_1_1: To date, the specific cause of Pityriasis rosea has not been established. Unlike many other skin conditions, this is not an allergic reaction, and the fungal or bacterial nature of the rash has not been established either.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_1_2: Some dermatological schools consider viral etiology, in particular, hermetic infection, but this has not been conclusively proven.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_1: The rash often begins with a single round or oval pink patch with a raised margin (harbinger, maternal plaque). Later, starting in the central part of this spot, peeling appears, and the color becomes yellow.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_2: The size of the maternal plaque is approximately 2-10 cm.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_3: After a few days or weeks, grouped smaller oval pink spots from 1 to 2 cm appear on the abdomen, chest, back, arms and legs. These spots can spread to the neck, very rarely to the face. Gradually, barely noticeable dry folded scales appear in the center of the spots, and a border without peeling is noted along the periphery.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_4: Spots on the back are often oval or elongated, and are located vertically and at an angle in relation to the spine, which gives the appearance of “spruce”.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_5: About half of patients with Pityriasis rosea develop mild itching, which does not cause serious problems, but with a prolonged course of the disease, it can worsen the quality of life.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_6: The rash usually lasts 6 to 8 weeks, but it can last for several months.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_7: In rare cases, the rash can take on other forms. Round papules can be seen in young children, pregnant women, and people with dark skin. Blisters (vesicular rash) can occur in infants and young children. In some people, maternal plaque may be absent or two may be present.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_2_8: Before the onset of the disease, patients usually notice a feeling of fatigue or flu-like symptoms: headache, sore throat, loss of appetite, weakness, nausea.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_4_1: If the diagnosis is unclear, additional tests may be done to exclude fungal skin lesions (potassium hydroxide (KOH test)) or other diseases (culturing, biopsy).
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_4_2: A visual examination is often sufficient to diagnose Pityriasis rosea. However, the diagnosis process can be difficult when only the precursor (maternal plaque) is visible. During this period of the disease, Pityriasis rosea is often mistaken for ringworm or eczema. After the appearance of a small rash, the diagnosis becomes obvious.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_3_1: A rash with Pityriasis rosea can be similar to the rash seen with other skin conditions, including ringworm, tinea versicolor, eczema, and psoriasis.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_3_2: A similar rash can be a manifestation of intolerance to certain medications or exposure to other toxic substances on the body.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_3_3: A rash on the palms or soles of the feet can be a sign of a more serious condition than Pityriasis rosea. In such situations, a dermatologist’s examination is required.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_5_1: Usually, Pityriasis rosea does not require special treatment: the rash goes away on its own in 1-3 months. If itching occurs, special lotions may be prescribed. When severe symptoms of inflammation, severe itching appear, local anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids are used.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_5_2: Antiviral drugs (such as acyclovir) are sometimes prescribed. Early initiation of these drugs (early in the onset of the rash) can shorten the duration of the illness and the severity of symptoms.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_5_3: If the rash persists for more than 3 months, a mandatory follow-up appointment with a dermatologist is required.
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_desc_5_4: Reducing the severity of itching at home:
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_li_5_1: Exclude overheating and high temperatures in the room
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_li_5_3: Cool or warm showers (avoid hot baths)
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_li_5_4: Using over-the-counter hydrocortisone creams to treat small itchy areas (strictly according to the instructions)
pityriasis_rosea.pityriasis_rosea_li_5_7: For the period of illness, use only mild, gentle soaps (for example, baby soap)

pustular_psoriasis.pustular_psoriasis_desc_1: Pustular psoriasis is a form of psoriasis (referred to as an independent disease by some medical schools), a chronic inflammatory skin disease that is the presence of white pustules on the skin. Has a more severe course compared to simple psoriasis.
